backport.subject: Avoid state corruption via bailout
backport.author: Arnaud Le Blanc
files_list: Zend/zend_API.h, zend_alloc.h, zend_hash.h, zend_llist.c, zend_multiply.h, zend_strtod.c, zend_vm_execute.h

where.layer: The language a site is written in (PHP code)
where.text: Not where the bug is. A site's own PHP code can be perfect; php2shell.com's phrase is that a 'Hello World' application on an affected version is affected.

where.layer: The Zend engine (C): memory manager, request start-up and shutdown
where.text: Where both bugs are. Zend/zend_alloc.c is PHP's allocator; main/main.c runs a request's start-up and shutdown; main/rfc1867.c parses multipart bodies; main/php_variables.c registers $_GET, $_POST and friends; ext/session/session.c hooks the multipart parser for upload progress. All C.

where.layer: The SAPI (how PHP is attached to the web server)
where.text: Where exploitability differs. mod_php runs request shutdown even when start-up failed, 'before any application-specific code begins execution'; FPM is susceptible by source analysis; the fix touches sapi/ in five files.

where.layer: The web server, the WAF, the operating system
where.text: Not where the bug is, but where the controls are: a WAF matches the request shape, the OS limits what the worker can do once it is code execution.

mechanism.text: When a request pushed PHP past memory_limit, the allocator called zend_mm_safe_error, which raised a fatal error inside a zend_try and then called zend_bailout(): a C longjmp back to the request's top-level handler. The jump abandons whatever function was half-way through building request state. On mod_php the request shutdown then runs anyway and reads that half-built state. That is CVE-2026-109618, 'RCE via OOM corruption'. The same longjmp, or any fatal error, could leave global state pointing into request memory that is about to be freed; the next request on the same worker reads it. That is CVE-2026-109619, 'RCE via stale global state'.

The attacker needs to make the allocator fail at a moment of their choosing. The confirmed ways are request-shaped: a multipart body with many parts or long headers (rfc1867.c), deeply nested form field names (php_variables.c and the hash table), and the session upload-progress feature, which is on by default and does work inside the multipart parser before the application runs. Several vendors say the exploit also needs to know the running binary's layout on x86_64, which is why the CVSS vector says attack complexity high.

mechanism.step: After the fix: the soft limit
mechanism.text: zend_mm_check_limit no longer jumps. If an allocation would exceed memory_limit (now the soft limit), it queues a 'delayed OOM' error and lets the allocation succeed. At the next VM safe point zend_handle_delayed_oom runs, throws an UnwindExit that unwinds the PHP frames in an orderly way, and raises the fatal error with the request's state intact. The commit's own comment: 'When the soft limit is to be exceeded, a delayed OOM error is queued. When the hard limit is to be exceeded, the function does not return.'

mechanism.step: After the fix: the hard limit
mechanism.text: A new memory_hard_limit_percent setting defines a ceiling above memory_limit. Reaching it calls zend_mm_hard_limit_error and the process ends with _exit(), with no cleanup to corrupt. Allocations that callers can tolerate failing become 'fallible' and return NULL instead of jumping. zend_mm_panic now also uses _exit rather than exit.

shutdown_executor, php_request_shutdown and sapi_deactivate set the pointers they free to NULL or UNDEF ('may be accessed before php_request_startup()'), so a later request cannot find stale state. A new max_multipart_body_parts setting bounds the number of parts the parser will accept; the multipart header parser keeps only Content-Disposition and Content-Type and ignores duplicates; the session upload-progress callback is changed.

Every place in the engine and the bundled extensions that used to say 'allocation failed, bail out' had to be rewritten to the new contract: queue the error, fail the allocation, or hit the hard limit. That is why ext/standard, mbstring, gd, date and soap are in the diff, and why the PHP Foundation says the fix 'required a major change to the PHP engine' and took two months.

The end-of-life backport is a different, smaller change (17 engine files): it makes every memory error exit the process immediately (zend_mm_safe_error_ex calling _exit) instead of unwinding, resets the same globals, caps multipart parts and disables the session upload-progress callback outright. It is labelled 'Minimal mitigation for EOL version' in the commit. A worker that _exits on every OOM is safe from this bug class and worse at availability.

open: Which of the 389 files are the security fix and which are the refactor the fix needed is not separable from the diff alone; the GHSA text and the commit body are the only guide.

The 2024 trail: the Foundation says a core developer saw the first signs of the OOM problem while fixing a 2024 audit finding. That developer, that fix and that issue are not named in any captured source, and this site's shallow clone does not reach 2024 history.
Whether the Fediverse report of an incomplete fix in 8.5.12 concerns one of these paths.
